title: Git and GitHub for Beginners
summary: Learn what version control is and use commits, branches, merges and pull requests, either in a phone browser on GitHub or with basic Git commands.
audience: Beginners aged 14 and up. No prior coding needed. A phone, tablet or computer with a browser is enough for most lessons

lessons.title: What version control is and why it matters

body.p: Imagine a group of students writing a science project together. One person saves report-final.docx, another saves report-final-v2.docx, and a third saves report-final-REALLY-final.docx. Soon nobody knows which file is correct, and someone's good work is overwritten. Version control solves this problem. It is a system that records every change to a set of files, who made it, when, and why, and lets you go back to any earlier moment.

body.h: Git and GitHub are not the same thing

list: Git is the version control tool. It runs on your own device and keeps the history of your project.
GitHub is a website that stores Git projects online so that you can back them up, share them and work with other people. Other sites do a similar job, but this course uses GitHub.

body.p: You can use Git without GitHub, and you can do many GitHub tasks without ever typing a Git command, because GitHub lets you work from its website in a browser. That matters if you only have a phone or tablet: you can complete most of this course in a mobile browser.

list: Repository (repo): a project folder together with its full history. On GitHub, a repo is the page that holds your project.
Commit: a saved snapshot of your files at a moment in time, with a short message describing what changed. Think of it as a save point in a video game.
Branch: a separate line of work. You can try an idea on a branch without disturbing the main version.
Merge: combining the work from one branch into another.
Pull request: a request on GitHub asking for your branch to be merged, so others can review it first.
Remote: a copy of the repository stored somewhere else, usually on GitHub.
Clone: download a full copy of a remote repository.

body.p: Fatima, Chidi and Wanjiru are building a class website. Fatima writes the home page and makes a commit with the message Add home page. Chidi creates a branch called contact-page and adds a contact page there. Wanjiru adds a style file on another branch. Each person works without breaking the others. When their work is ready, it is merged together. If a mistake appears next week, the history shows exactly which commit introduced it, and the project can be returned to the commit before it.

Each commit has a unique identifier called a hash, a long string of letters and digits. Git usually shows only the first seven characters. This is the sort of list you will see later when you run a command that shows history. The hashes below are examples; yours will be different.

body.code:
1a42927 Add contact page
8e3c0b4 Add home page
5d7f9a1 Create project

body.p: The newest commit is at the top. Good commit messages are short and clear, written like a heading that finishes the sentence: this commit will... For example, Fix broken link on About page tells your future self far more than Update or stuff.

body.tip: Commit small and often. A commit that does one thing is easy to understand and easy to undo. A commit called Changed everything is hard to review and hard to fix.

lessons.title: Using GitHub from a browser or phone

body.p: You can learn all the main ideas of Git using only the GitHub website. It works in a mobile browser, though a larger screen or the browser's desktop-site option can make it easier. Button names and positions on GitHub change from time to time, so this lesson describes what to do rather than quoting exact labels. Look for the control that does the action described.

body.h: Create an account and a repository

steps: Open the GitHub website in your browser and create a free account, using an email address you can access and a strong password.
Find the control for creating a new repository, usually a plus sign near the top of the page.
Give the repository a short name without spaces, such as my-first-repo. Use hyphens instead of spaces.
Choose whether it is public (anyone can see it) or private (only people you allow). Never store passwords or private information in a public repo.
Choose the option to add a README file, then create the repository.

body.p: The new repo page shows your files, and README.md is already there. A README is the front page of your project: it explains what the project is and how to use it. The ending .md means Markdown, a simple way of writing formatted text, where a line beginning with # becomes a heading.
Open README.md and look for the pencil or edit control. Add a few lines, for example a heading and a sentence about yourself.

body.code:
# My First Repo

Hello from Lagos! I am learning Git and GitHub.

- Learn commits
- Learn branches

body.p: When you finish, find the button that saves your changes as a commit. GitHub shows a box for a commit message. Write a short, clear message, such as Add introduction to README. There is also a choice between committing directly to the current branch or creating a new branch. For now, commit directly to the main branch. After you confirm, your change is a commit, and it appears in the history.

To add a new file, look for an add file control on the repo page and choose to create a new file. Type the file name, including its ending, such as notes.txt or index.html, then type the content and commit it as before. You can include a folder by typing its name followed by a slash in the file name box, such as docs/plan.txt. To bring in files you already have, such as a picture or document on your phone, choose the upload option, select the files from your device, and commit them with a message.

Find the control labelled with a clock or the word commits on the repo page. You will see each commit with its message, author and time. Open one to see exactly which lines were added in green and removed in red. This view is called a diff.

body.code:
- Learn commits
+ Learn commits and branches

body.p: A line starting with minus was removed and a line starting with plus was added. A changed line appears as one removal and one addition.

body.tip: Practise: create a repo called practice, add a README, then make three separate commits: edit the README, add a notes.txt file, and upload a photo. Then open the history and check that you see three commits plus the first one.

lessons.title: The command line: your first local repository

body.p: The same ideas can be done with commands in a terminal on a computer. If you only have a phone, read this lesson to understand what the tools do; you will recognise the same actions on the website. Commands are exact, so type them carefully. Lines starting with a dollar sign show what you type; do not type the dollar sign. Lines without it are the output Git prints.
Git labels every commit with a name and an email address. Set them once on each computer. Use your own details.

body.code:
$ git config --global user.name "Amina Bello"
$ git config --global user.email "amina@example.com"

body.h: Create a repository and check its state

body.code:
$ mkdir my-project
$ cd my-project
$ git init -b main
$ git status

Initialized empty Git repository in /home/amina/my-project/.git/
On branch main

No commits yet

nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)

body.p: The command git init turns the current folder into a repository by creating a hidden folder named .git where the history lives. Do not delete that folder. The option -b main names the first branch main (it needs Git 2.28 or newer; on older versions just run git init); without it, the default name depends on your Git settings. The git status command is the one you will use most. Run it whenever you are unsure what is going on.

body.h: The three places: working folder, staging area, repository

body.p: Git does not commit every change automatically. You choose which changes go into the next commit by staging them first. Your files live in the working folder, git add copies chosen changes to the staging area, and git commit saves everything in the staging area as a permanent snapshot.

body.code:
$ echo "Study timetable" > plan.txt
$ git status
$ git add plan.txt
$ git status
$ git commit -m "Add study timetable"

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	plan.txt

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
	new file:   plan.txt

[main (root-commit) 1a42927] Add study timetable
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 plan.txt

body.p: The output above is trimmed to the important lines. The first status shows plan.txt as untracked, meaning Git has seen it but is not recording it. After git add it is listed under changes to be committed. After git commit, status says there is nothing to commit and the working tree is clean. The -m option gives the commit message in quotation marks. The hash in your output will differ from the one shown.

body.code: $ git log --oneline
1a42927 Add study timetable

body.p: Each further commit adds a line at the top. Use git add . to stage all changes in the current folder, but check git status first so you do not stage something by mistake. Another useful command is git diff, which shows changes you have made but not yet staged.

body.tip: The cycle you will repeat all the time is: edit files, git status, git add, git commit. If you forget the staging step, your commit will not include the changes.

body.p: A branch is an independent line of commits. The default branch is usually called main and should hold work that is known to be good. When you want to add a feature or try an idea, you create a new branch, work there, and merge it back when you are happy. If the idea fails, you simply delete the branch and main is untouched.

body.code:
$ git branch
$ git switch -c add-contact
$ git branch

* main
Switched to a new branch 'add-contact'
* add-contact
  main

body.p: Git branch lists branches, and the star marks the one you are on. The command git switch -c add-contact creates the branch and moves you to it. The first listing shows only main. After the switch, the second listing shows both branches, with the star now on add-contact. Always check with git status or git branch which branch you are on before you edit. To go back, use git switch main. Older tutorials use git checkout for the same job, for example git checkout main and git checkout -b add-contact, and those still work.

body.h: Work on the branch, then merge

body.code:
$ echo "Contact: school@example.com" > contact.txt
$ git add contact.txt
$ git commit -m "Add contact page"
$ git switch main
$ git merge add-contact

Updating 1a42927..7107ab3
Fast-forward
 contact.txt | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 contact.txt

body.p: You merge by first switching to the branch that should receive the work, here main, and then running git merge with the name of the branch to bring in. Here main had no new commits of its own, so Git simply moved main forward to the end of add-contact. This is called a fast-forward. When both branches have new commits, Git creates a merge commit that joins them. After a successful merge you can delete the finished branch with git branch -d add-contact.

A conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines of the same file differently. Git cannot guess which version you want, so it stops and asks you. Suppose main says the club meets on Friday and the ama branch says Tuesday. After git merge ama, Git reports a conflict and puts both versions in the file.

body.code:
Title: Maths Club
<<<<<<< HEAD
Meets: Friday
=======
Meets: Tuesday
>>>>>>> ama

body.p: The part between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is the version on your current branch. The part between ======= and >>>>>>> ama is the version being merged in. To resolve the conflict, edit the file so that it contains exactly the text you want and delete the three marker lines. Then finish the merge.

body.code:
$ git add notes.txt
$ git commit -m "Resolve meeting day conflict"

body.p: Conflicts are normal, not a sign that you did something wrong. Talk to your teammate if you are not sure which version is right.

body.tip: If you ever see the marker lines <<<<<<<, ======= or >>>>>>> in a file, a conflict is waiting to be resolved. Never commit a file that still contains them.

lessons.title: Branches and pull requests on GitHub

body.p: On a team, nobody should push untested changes straight into main. Instead each person works on a branch, then opens a pull request. A pull request, often shortened to PR, is a proposal on GitHub: here are my commits on this branch, please review them and merge them into main. Teammates can read the changes, comment on specific lines, and approve. Everything below can be done in a mobile browser.

body.h: Make a branch and a change in the browser

steps: Open your repository on GitHub and find the branch selector, a drop-down near the top left of the file list that shows the current branch name, probably main.
Type a new branch name, such as improve-readme, and choose the option to create that branch from main.
Confirm that the selector now shows improve-readme. Every edit you make now goes to this branch only.
Open README.md, use the edit control, add a new line such as the project goal, and commit your changes with a clear message. Make sure the commit goes to improve-readme and not to main.

body.p: GitHub often shows a banner suggesting you open a pull request after you push or commit to a new branch. If you do not see one, look for a pull requests tab on the repo page.

steps: Go to the pull requests area and choose to create a new pull request.
Set the base branch to main (where the changes should go) and the compare branch to improve-readme (where the changes are).
Scroll down to read the list of changed files and lines. This is your last chance to spot a mistake.
Write a clear title, for example Add project goal to README, and a short description of what and why.

body.p: The PR page shows your description, the commits, the changed files, and a conversation. A reviewer can write comments, and you can respond or push more commits to the same branch; the PR updates automatically.

When the changes are approved, use the merge control on the PR page and confirm. GitHub merges the branch into main. If GitHub reports that the branch has conflicts, you must resolve them first; GitHub has an editor for simple conflicts on its website, which shows the same marker lines you met in lesson 4. After merging, GitHub offers to delete the branch; that is safe, because the commits are now in main.

If you do not have permission to change someone else's repo, you fork it first. A fork is your own copy of the repository under your account. You make a branch in your fork, then open a pull request from your fork back to the original. This is how people from all over the world contribute to open-source projects.

body.tip: A good pull request is small and has a clear title. Reviewers can understand ten changed lines in two minutes, but five hundred changed lines in one PR often go unread.

lessons.title: Push, pull, clone and a good README

body.p: So far your local repository and GitHub have been separate worlds. A remote connects them. The remote that points to your GitHub copy is conventionally named origin. Three commands move commits between your device and GitHub: push sends your new commits up, pull brings new commits down, and clone makes a first full copy.

body.code:
$ git clone https://github.com/your-username/my-first-repo.git
$ cd my-first-repo
$ git log --oneline

body.p: Replace your-username with your own account name, and copy the exact address from the code or clone control on your repository page. Clone downloads all files and the full history, and sets origin for you.

body.h: Push a local repository to GitHub

body.p: If you created a repo locally with git init, first create an empty repository on GitHub, without a README, and copy its address. Then connect and push.

body.code:
$ git remote add origin https://github.com/your-username/my-project.git
$ git push -u origin main

body.p: Git remote add origin gives the remote a name and an address. Git push -u origin main sends the main branch to origin; the -u option remembers the link, so later you can type just git push. GitHub does not accept your account password for pushes from the command line. You sign in using a method that GitHub provides, such as a personal access token, a credential helper, or an SSH key. Follow GitHub's current help pages for the setup, because the steps change over time.

body.h: Pull to stay up to date

body.p: If a teammate merges a pull request on GitHub, your local copy does not know. Before you start work each day, update it.

body.code:
$ git switch main
$ git pull

body.p: Git pull downloads new commits from origin and merges them into your current branch. If you have made local commits at the same time that conflict with the remote ones, you will resolve conflicts exactly as in lesson 4.

A README is the first thing a visitor sees. Keep it short and useful. A good one answers four questions: what is this project, how do I use or run it, who made it, and how can I contribute or contact you. Here is an example for a class project.

body.code:
# Rainfall Tracker

A small web page that records daily rainfall at our school in Freetown.

## How to use

1. Open index.html in a browser.
2. Type today's rainfall in millimetres.

## Authors

Class 10B science club

body.p: In Markdown, one # gives a main heading and two ## give a subheading. Numbered lines make an ordered list, and a line starting with a hyphen makes a bullet. Make your README the front door to your project and your portfolio, since employers and universities often look at GitHub profiles.

body.tip: Never commit passwords, tokens, exam results or other private data. Once something is in a commit it stays in history even if you delete the file later, and in a public repo anyone can read it.

quiz.q: Three students keep emailing each other files called project-v2.docx and project-final.docx and overwriting each other's work. Which statement best describes how Git helps?
options: It records each change as a commit, so old versions can be recovered and nobody silently overwrites work
It scans every file for spelling and grammar mistakes and corrects them before anyone can save a copy
It compresses the project files so they are small enough to attach to each email without errors
It gives every student a separate password for each file so that only one person can open it at once

quiz.q: Which statement about Git and GitHub is correct?
options: Git is a website that stores projects online, and GitHub is a program installed on your computer
Git is the version control tool, and GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories online
They are two names for the same program, and GitHub is simply the newer release of Git
GitHub must be installed first, because Git commands cannot run on a device without an account

quiz.q: Which commit message is the most useful to a teammate reading the history?
options: Update
Changes
stuff
Fix broken link on the About page

quiz.q: You are editing README.md in the GitHub website on your phone. What turns your edits into a commit?
options: Closing the browser tab, which saves the draft as a new commit
Using the save-changes control and confirming with a commit message
Refreshing the page so GitHub records the edit under your name
Typing git commit -m into the file editor and then pressing enter

quiz.q: You create plan.txt in your repository folder and run git status. What does Git report about it?
options: It is committed, because it sits in the repository folder
It is deleted, because Git has no earlier copy of it
It is untracked, because Git is not yet recording it
It is staged, ready to commit, because it was just created

quiz.q: A student edits report.txt, then runs git commit -m "Update report" without git add. What happens?
options: Nothing is committed, because the change was never staged
The change is committed and also pushed to GitHub at once
Git asks which branch to use and then commits all changes
The file is deleted from the folder, because it was edited

quiz.q: What is the correct order of commands for saving a new change in a local repo?
options: git commit, then git add, then edit the file
git add, then edit the file, then git commit
Edit the file, then git add, then git commit
git push, then edit the file, then git commit

quiz.q: You are on main and run git switch -c add-quiz. What has happened?
options: main has been deleted and replaced by a branch named add-quiz
A new branch named add-quiz was created and you are now on it
The add-quiz branch was merged into main and then removed
Your changes were pushed to a new add-quiz branch on GitHub

quiz.q: You finished work on the add-contact branch and want it in main. Which commands do this?
options: git switch add-contact, then git merge main
git branch -d main, then git merge add-contact
git merge add-contact while on add-contact
git switch main, then git merge add-contact

quiz.q:
After a merge, a file contains these lines:
<<<<<<< HEAD
Meets: Friday
=======
Meets: Tuesday
>>>>>>> ama
What is the correct way to resolve this?
options: Commit the file as it is, because Git picks the newest line automatically
Delete the whole file and commit, so that Git forgets both versions
Keep the text you want, delete all marker lines, then git add and git commit
Run git init again in the folder, so that Git rebuilds the file's history
A command that downloads the newest commits from GitHub and merges them into your local branch
A message asking GitHub staff to delete a repository that you no longer use
A copy of someone else's repository saved under your own account so you can edit it freely
A proposal on GitHub to merge one branch into another, so others can review it first

quiz.q: When opening a pull request that should add improve-readme to main, which setting is correct?
options: Base: improve-readme, compare: main
Base: main, compare: improve-readme
Base and compare are both main
Base and compare are both improve-readme

quiz.q: A teammate merged a pull request on GitHub this morning. What should you run to update your local main?
options: git init
git push
git pull
git add .

quiz.q: You made a repository on your own computer with git init. Which pair of commands connects it to an empty GitHub repository and uploads the main branch?
options: git clone <address>, then git pull origin main
git remote add origin <address>, then git push -u origin main
git checkout origin, then git merge main origin
git status -u, then git log origin/main

quiz.q: A student commits a file containing her email password to a public repo, then deletes the file in the next commit. Is the password safe?
options: Yes, because the later commit removes the file from every earlier commit in the repository
Yes, because only people who follow her account on the website can open the repository
Only if she also renames the repository, because old commits are then hidden from visitors
No, it remains in the history for anyone to read, so she must change the password
